title: Six Years of Watching
subtitle: Active surveillance of a papillary carcinoma, and the day it ended
description: Reading a thyroid panel after a suspicious aspirate, choosing a needle for a posteriorly placed nodule, recognizing when active surveillance has failed, preoperative documentation, preoperative imaging, ATA recurrence risk with an aggressive histological variant, and what follows a lobectomy.

steps.title: Step 1/7: The Panel After a Suspicious Aspirate
steps.scenario:
A 44-year-old woman is referred to your clinic with a right thyroid nodule found on a neck ultrasound. She has no compressive symptoms, no voice change, no radiation history and no family history of thyroid cancer.

Her thyroid panel (institutional reference range in brackets):

    TSH                     1.76 uIU/mL      [0.34 - 5.60]
    Free T4                 0.98 ng/dL       [0.61 - 1.44]
    T3                      105 ng/dL        [87 - 178]
    Anti-TPO antibody       40.2 IU/mL   (H) [< 34]
    Thyroglobulin           > 300 ng/mL  (H) [1.4 - 78]
    Anti-thyroglobulin      1.8 IU/mL        [< 4]
    TSH receptor antibody   0.8 IU/L         [< 1.75]
steps.question: How do you read this panel?

options.text: (A) A thyroglobulin above 300 ng/mL indicates a high tumor burden and argues for prompt surgery
(B) The raised anti-TPO points to thyroiditis and makes malignancy less likely
(C) The normal TSH means the nodule is not autonomously functioning; nothing else here changes the plan
(D) The normal anti-thyroglobulin antibody means the thyroglobulin can be trusted as a tumor marker

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

TSH is the only test here that changes the pathway. If suppressed, it suggests an autonomously functioning nodule, rarely malignant, and leads to scintigraphy rather than a needle. If normal, as here, and the decision depends on ultrasound and cytology. Free T4 and T3 grade dysfunction only once TSH is abnormal; the TSH receptor antibody matters only if TSH is suppressed.

Nothing on this panel diagnoses cancer. Only calcitonin can, for medullary carcinoma, and it was not ordered.

Why the others fail:
(A) Thyroglobulin is produced by all follicular thyroid tissue, so its level reflects gland volume, thyroiditis, and even mechanical disruption from palpation or biopsy  (it is not specific to malignancy). While the thyroid gland is still in place, no single Tg threshold reliably distinguishes benign from malignant disease; overlap between the two is substantial, and current ATA guidelines do not recommend routine preoperative Tg or TgAb testing for diagnostic purposes. TG only becomes clinically actionable once the gland and all Tg-producing tissue  has been removed. That is why a preoperative Tg is drawn: not to diagnose or stage disease, but to establish an individual baseline. After thyroidectomy, serial Tg measurements (and their trend over time relative to that baseline and TSH stimulation status) are used to predict persistent, recurrent, or metastatic differentiated thyroid cancer. 
(B) Anti-TPO establishes thyroiditis and predicts hypothyroidism after lobectomy, but does not lower the risk of a discrete suspicious nodule.
(D) Anti-Tg tells you whether the thyroglobulin can be believed, since it falsely lowers Tg in standard assays. A true value is still not a tumor marker.

Keypoint: the TSH tells you which pathway to follow, the antibodies tell you about the gland, and the thyroglobulin tells you nothing until the thyroid is removed.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020. Giovanella L, D'Aurizio F, Petranovic Ovcaricek P, Gorges R. Diagnostic, theranostic and prognostic value of thyroglobulin in thyroid cancer. J Clin Med. 2024;13(9):2463. doi:10.3390/jcm13092463.

steps.title: Step 2/7: Long Enough to Reach
steps.scenario:
You scan her yourself. The right lobe contains a 0.81 x 0.71 x 0.61 cm nodule: solid, markedly hypoechoic, ill-defined with an irregular boundary and an incomplete halo.

It sits against the posterior border of the lobe, deep to the bulk of the gland.

You aspirate it under your own ultrasound guidance.

Load image 2: A 22 gauge and a 25 gauge needle side by side against a ruler. Caption: 'Needle gauges.'

steps.question: Which needle do you use?

options.text: (A) 25 to 27 gauge
(B) 22 to 23 gauge
(C) 18 gauge core needle
(D) 20 gauge with continuous strong suction

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The needle has to do two things at once. It has to be thin, because blood in the sample is the main reason an aspirate comes back non-diagnostic. It also has to be long enough to reach a nodule sitting at the back of the lobe. The thinnest needles are also the shortest ones, so 22 to 23 gauge is the compromise.

Why the others fail:
(A) This is the right choice for a nodule near the surface. This one is too deep, and a needle that does not reach the target brings back normal thyroid tissue instead.
(C) A core needle is used when repeated fine needle samples are non-diagnostic, or when lymphoma is suspected. Neither applies here.
(D) Blood in the sample comes mostly from suction and from bleeding, not from the size of the needle. Strong continuous suction is the quickest way to spoil the specimen.

Keypoint: choose the needle by how deep the nodule is, not by how suspicious it looks.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.

steps.title: Step 3/7: The Day Surveillance Ends
steps.scenario:
The cytology returns papillary thyroid carcinoma.

The nodule measures 0.51 x 0.63 x 0.58 cm. Below 1 cm it is size-eligible for active surveillance, and after discussion she chooses it.

Six months later:

    Baseline     0.51 x 0.63 x 0.58 cm
    6 months     0.81 x 0.83 x 0.90 cm

On the follow-up scan the lesion now abuts the posterior thyroid capsule.
steps.media: Load image: Side-by-side ultrasound, baseline and six-month study, matched plane and scale. Caption: 'Baseline and six months.'
steps.question: Which finding ends active surveillance?

options.text: (A) The maximal diameter has increased by more than 3 mm
(B) The nodule is approaching the 1 cm ceiling for surveillance
(C) The nodule grew during the very first surveillance interval
(D) Growth of more than 3 mm in one dimension and a volume increase over 50 percent, in a lesion now abutting the posterior capsule

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

Two NCCN triggers are met here, and a third finding supports them.

NCCN lists growth of 3 mm or more in any dimension, or a volume increase of 50 percent or more, as reasons to move from surveillance to surgical consultation, alongside new biopsy-proven nodal metastasis, distant metastasis, or radiologic extrathyroidal extension. Her longitudinal dimension went from 0.58 to 0.90 cm, an increase of 3.2 mm. Her volume went from 0.098 to 0.317 mL, an increase of over 200 percent. The lesion also now abuts the posterior capsule, close to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Why the others fail:
(A) The maximal diameter went from 0.63 to 0.90 cm, which is 2.7 mm. The 3 mm threshold is met in a different dimension, not this one.
(B) 0.90 cm is close to 1 cm, but size alone is not a trigger. The listed triggers are growth, nodal or distant metastasis, and extrathyroidal extension.
(C) Some growth is expected. Surveillance is built around defined thresholds rather than around any change at all.

Keypoint: measure every dimension and calculate the volume, because the threshold may be crossed on an axis you were not watching.

Reference: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Thyroid Carcinoma (add the version you are working from). Tuttle RM, Fagin JA, Minkowitz G, et al. Natural history and tumor volume kinetics of papillary thyroid cancers during active surveillance. JAMA Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2017;143(10):1015-1020.

steps.title: Step 4/7: Before Surgery
steps.scenario: She agrees to a right thyroidectomy with isthmusectomy. She has no voice complaint and no prior neck surgery. You plan to use intraoperative nerve monitoring.
steps.question: What must be documented before she goes to surgery?

options.text: (A) Vocal fold mobility on laryngoscopy, and a baseline thyroglobulin with anti-thyroglobulin antibody
(B) Vocal fold mobility only; a thyroglobulin in an intact gland has no use at any stage
(C) A baseline calcium and parathyroid hormone, since hypoparathyroidism is the main risk of the procedure
(D) Nothing further; she has no voice complaint, and nerve monitoring will identify the nerve intraoperatively

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Laryngoscopy is done to record the preoperative baseline of vocal fold mobility. A normal voice does not mean both folds move normally. If a fold is found to be immobile after the operation and there is no record from before, it cannot be determined whether the surgery caused it.

The thyroglobulin is drawn for a different reason than in Step 1. It is not being used to diagnose or stage the cancer. It is there to record her starting value. Tg only becomes useful once all thyroid tissue has been removed. After that, the trend in her Tg levels, compared with this starting value and with her TSH at the time, is what shows whether disease is still present or has come back. The antibody is drawn at the same time so those later results can be interpreted.

Why the others fail:
(B) This is right about what Tg means for diagnosis and wrong about why it is being drawn. It is a starting value, not a test.
(C) Hypoparathyroidism is uncommon when only one lobe is removed, and a baseline calcium would not change the operation.
(D) Nerve monitoring helps find the nerve during the operation and gives information about it at the end. It cannot tell you what the vocal fold was doing beforehand.

Keypoint: record the vocal folds before the operation, and draw the thyroglobulin as a starting value rather than as a test.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985. Giovanella L, D'Aurizio F, Petranovic Ovcaricek P, Gorges R. J Clin Med. 2024;13(9):2463. doi:10.3390/jcm13092463.

steps.title: Step 5/7: Which Imaging
steps.scenario: The lesion abuts the posterior thyroid capsule, which raises the question of extrathyroidal extension. Her ultrasound shows no abnormal cervical nodes.
steps.media: Load image: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck at the level of the thyroid, unannotated. Caption: 'Axial, post-contrast.'
steps.question: What imaging do you obtain before the operation?

options.text: (A) Non-contrast CT, to avoid an iodine load before possible radioiodine
(B) No cross-sectional imaging; the ultrasound already covers the neck
(C) Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and mediastinum
(D) Repeat ultrasound of the lateral compartments, since ultrasound is the most sensitive test for cervical nodes

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

The 2025 ATA guidelines recommend a CT or MRI of the neck and chest with intravenous contrast before surgery when there is gross extrathyroidal extension, extensive or bulky lymph nodes, or a suspicion that the airway, esophagus or chest is involved (strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence). Her nodule is touching the capsule, which raises the question of extrathyroidal extension, so she meets the criteria.

Why the others fail:
(A) Without contrast the scan cannot show whether the tumor is wrapped around vessels, or whether lymph nodes are enhancing or necrotic, and those are the findings that change the operation. The iodine clears in 4 to 6 weeks, and the ATA position is that better images are worth a short delay to radioiodine. A urine iodine level can be checked if there is doubt.
(B) Ultrasound cannot see the retropharyngeal, parapharyngeal, infraclavicular or mediastinal areas, and it cannot show how far the disease extends downward.
(D) Ultrasound is very good for the lateral neck, which is how she was staged N0. The problem is the areas it cannot reach.

Keypoint: contrast is necessary here, because the findings that would change the operation cannot be seen without it.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985, Recommendation 8.

steps.title: Step 6/7: Reading the Report
steps.scenario:
Final pathology:

    Papillary thyroid carcinoma, tall cell subtype, well differentiated
    Two foci, right lobe: 1.1 cm and 0.3 cm
    Extrathyroidal extension: not identified
    Vascular and lymphatic invasion: not identified
    Margin: tumor close to peripheral margin, less than 0.1 mm
    Lymph nodes: perithyroid 0/1, level VI 0/2
    pT1b(m) pN0
steps.media: Load image: Final pathology report, all patient and institutional identifiers redacted. Caption: 'Final histology.'
steps.question: Where does she fall in the ATA recurrence risk stratification?

options.text: (A) Low risk, because the tumor is intrathyroidal, node-negative and under 2 cm
(B) Intermediate risk, because of the tall cell subtype
(C) Intermediate risk, because the tumor is multifocal
(D) High risk, because the margin is less than 0.1 mm

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The ATA divides recurrence risk into low, intermediate and high.

Intermediate risk includes microscopic extrathyroidal extension, lymph node metastases, radioiodine-avid foci in the neck, vascular invasion, and aggressive histology. Tall cell is one of the named aggressive types, along with hobnail and columnar cell. That one feature puts her in the intermediate group even though everything else in the report looks favorable.

Why the others fail:
(A) To be low risk, the tumor must be confined to the thyroid with no aggressive histology, no vascular invasion, no extrathyroidal extension and no lymph node metastases. She meets all of those except the histology.
(C) A multifocal papillary carcinoma confined to the thyroid, with no other adverse features, stays in the low-risk group. Multifocality on its own does not change the category.
(D) High risk requires gross extrathyroidal extension, tumor left behind at surgery, distant metastases, or a lymph node 3 cm or larger. A close margin with no tumor at the edge is none of these.

Keypoint: check the histological type before assigning the risk category, because it can outweigh the size, the stage and the lymph node result.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985.

steps.title: Step 7/7: What Happens Now
steps.scenario: She has had a right thyroidectomy with isthmusectomy. The left lobe is intact. She asks what happens next.
steps.question: What do you recommend?

options.text: (A) Proceed to radioiodine ablation now
(B) Start levothyroxine and titrate to suppress TSH below 0.1 microIU/mL
(C) Annual ultrasound alone, since a lobectomy is definitive for any tumor under 2 cm
(D) Discuss completion thyroidectomy, since the intermediate-risk features may warrant radioiodine and it cannot be given with a lobe in place

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

Three things in her report make a second operation worth discussing: the tall cell type, two separate tumors, and a margin of less than 0.1 mm. While the left lobe is still there, thyroglobulin cannot be used to look for residual disease, and radioiodine is not given until the rest of the thyroid has been removed. The surgical decision has to be made first.

The 2025 ATA guidelines list tall cell as one of the higher-risk papillary types where completion thyroidectomy may be worth considering after a lobectomy. NCCN takes the same approach for a close or positive margin, lymphatic invasion, or high-grade histology.

Why the others fail:
(A) Radioiodine cannot be planned while the other lobe is still in place, so the surgical decision comes first. Since 2015 radioiodine has also been used selectively rather than given to everyone after surgery.
(B) Keeping TSH below 0.1 is not recommended for low or intermediate risk disease unless there is evidence the cancer has returned. For an intermediate-risk patient with no evidence of disease the target is 0.1 to 0.5, or 0.5 to 2.0, depending on how she responds to treatment.
(C) This is the older approach. Until 2015, TSH was suppressed routinely in almost everyone after surgery for thyroid cancer. Current practice sets the target by risk category and by response to treatment. Below 0.1 is reserved for high-risk disease or for structural disease that is still present. An intermediate-risk patient with no evidence of disease sits higher, around 0.1 to 0.5, and after a lobectomy alone the usual aim is a TSH in the normal range. Long-term suppression also raises the risk of atrial fibrillation and lowers bone density.

Keypoint: decide how much thyroid to remove before deciding about radioiodine, because leaving a lobe rules radioiodine out.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985. NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Thyroid Carcinoma (add the version you are working from).
